pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/taŋ.ɡun/** — ​Korean ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**taŋ** — ‌The first ​syllable ​of Dangun, ‌carrying primary ​stress in ‌the romanised ​form.
- ‌**ɡun** — ​The middle ​syllable or ​element, pronounced ​with ​level pitch ‌in Korean.
- ​**-** — ‌The ​final syllable, ‌often closing ​in a ‌nasal or ​simple ‌vowel in ​the Korean ​reading.

For ‌the modern ‌speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation is: ​'TAHNG-goon' — ‌The initial ​consonant ​is an ‌unaspirated velar ​stop, closer ​to a ‌soft ​‘t’ than ‌to English ​‘d’; the ​final nasal ​closes ​the first ‌syllable. The ‌scholarly capital ​marks the ‌name ​as a ​proper noun.

‌Kindred and ‌historical forms ‌of ‌the name:

- ​**Hangul** — ‌단군 — ​the Korean ​script ​form.
- **Hanja** ‌— 檀君 ​— the ​Sino-Korean ​character form.

‌The initial ​consonant is ​an unaspirated ​velar ‌stop, closer ​to a ‌soft ‘t’ ​than to ‌English ​‘d’; the ‌final nasal ‌closes the ​first syllable. ​The ​scholarly capital ​marks the ‌name as ‌a proper ​noun.

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

domains.body:
**Dangun** ​is the ‌legendary founder ‌of Gojoseon ​and the ​first ​ancestor of ​the Korean ​people in ‌Korean tradition. ​The ​name means ‌"Lord of ​the sandalwood" ‌and belongs ​to ‌the domain ​"Founder of ​Korea, First ​King." Dangun ​is ​the son ‌of Hwanung, ​the heavenly ‌prince ​who descended ‌to earth, ​and Ungnyeo, ‌a bear ​who ‌became a ​woman after ​enduring one ‌hundred days ‌in ‌a cave ​eating garlic ​and mugwort. ‌He is ​said ​to have ‌founded the ​state of ​Gojoseon at ‌Asadal ​in 2333 ‌BCE, an ​event commemorated ​on National ​Foundation ​Day, 3 ‌October.[^1]

### Founder ‌of Gojoseon

​Dangun is ‌the ​mythic first ​king whose ‌reign marks ‌the beginning ‌of ‌Korean statehood.

### ​Son of ‌Hwanung and ​Ungnyeo

His ​birth ​unites heavenly ‌descent with ​the transformed ​earth-animal, ​modelling cosmic ‌and terrestrial ​harmony.

### Asadal

​The sacred ​capital ‌where Dangun ​established law, ‌agriculture, and ​the ordering ‌of ​the people.

### ‌Sansin

After ‌his long ​reign Dangun ​became ​a mountain ​spirit, still ‌invoked for ‌protection and ​prosperity.

sources.citation: Kim Pusik, Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms), 1145.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Dangun ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The sandalwood ​tree** ​— ‌Dang ​檀 ‌means ​sandalwood; ‌the ​tree ‌marks ​the ‌sacred ​descent place ​of ‌Hwanung.
- ‌**Bear ‌and ​tiger** ​— ‌The ​two ​animals ‌who ​underwent ​Hwanung's ‌trial; the ​bear's ‌perseverance ​became ​the ​origin ​of ‌the ‌Korean ​people.
- ‌**Garlic ​and ​mugwort** ‌— The ‌austere ‌foods ‌of ​transformation, ‌marking ​the ​passage ​from ‌animal ​to ​human ​and from ‌wilderness ​to ​culture.
- ​**Mountain ‌peak** ​— ‌The ​place ‌where ​Dangun ‌withdrew ‌and ​continues to ​dwell ​as ​a ‌protective ‌mountain ​spirit.

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

mythology.body:
The mythology ​of Dangun ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, ​shamanic ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ​such as ‌the Samguk ​Yusa. The ​narratives are ‌not merely ​stories; they ‌encode social ​values, ritual ‌obligations, and ​relationships between ​humans, nature, ​and the ​sacred. Some ​details vary ‌by region and ​by shamanic ‌lineage.[^1]

### The ​Bear and ‌the Tiger ​(Samguk Yusa)

‌Hwanung tested ​a bear ‌and a ​tiger by ​locking them ‌in a ‌cave with ‌only garlic ​and mugwort. ​The tiger ‌gave up, ​but the ​bear endured ‌one hundred ​days and ​became a ‌woman named Ungnyeo. ​Hwanung then ‌took her ​as his ​wife, and ​she bore ​Dangun.[^2]

### The ‌Founding of ‌Gojoseon (Foundation ​myth)

Dangun ‌established the ​capital at ​Asadal and ‌ruled over ‌Gojoseon for ‌one thousand ‌five hundred ​years. The ‌date traditionally ​given for ​the founding, ​3 October ‌2333 BCE, is ​celebrated as ​National Foundation ​Day.

### Dangun ‌Becomes Mountain ​Spirit (Apotheosis)

​At the ​end of ‌his reign ​Dangun left ‌the affairs ​of state ‌and withdrew ​into the ‌mountains, where ‌he became ​a sansin, ​a mountain ​deity who ​continues to ‌protect the ‌land and ​its people.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, or ‌artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex corpus ​is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Dangun with ​certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ​Korean name ‌of ​this ‌type ​the material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ‌be thin, ​and ​the ‌primary ‌evidence ‌remains the ​textual ​testimony ‌gathered ​in the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section[^1].

​Were ‌such evidence ​to ‌surface, ​it ​would ​take recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ‌or ​dedicatory inscriptions ‌naming ​단군 ​(檀君), ‌sanctuary ‌or cult ‌remains ‌tied ​to ‌founder ​of korea ​and ​iconography ‌matching ​its traditional ​attributes ​(the ‌sandalwood ​tree ​and bear ​and ‌tiger). ​Each ‌candidate would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the ‌reconstructed form ​of ​the ​name ​before ‌entering the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Dangun** ​(*dangun*) — ‌Founder ‌of Korea, ​First King ​· ​Lord of ​the ​sandalwood — ‌belongs to ​the ​Korean tradition, ‌where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Founder ​of ​Korea, First ​King". ​The name ​means ‌"Lord of ​the sandalwood"[^1].

‌**Dangun** ​is the ‌legendary ​founder of ‌Gojoseon and ​the ‌first ancestor ​of ​the Korean ‌people: ‌son of ‌the heavenly ​prince ​Hwanung and ‌the ​bear-woman Ungnyeo, ​king ‌of Asadal ​for fifteen ​hundred ‌mythic years, ​and ‌at last ​a mountain ​spirit ​watching over ​the ‌land from ‌every ​peak.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical ​scholarly spelling ‌**Dangun** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/dangun/). ‌The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ​form *dangun* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Hangul ​+ Hanja ​as ​**단군 ​(檀君)**. ‌Etymologically it ​means ​"Lord ‌of the ​sandalwood"[^1].

‌The ​canonical ‌spelling **Dangun** ​matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ​The ‌plain ​ASCII form ‌*dangun* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so ​no ‌lost diacritics ​or ​encoding ‌transition is ‌claimed. ‌The ​editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix ​one reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization and ​provenance, ‌and ​keep ​the original ​evidence ​visible. ‌The displayed ‌form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ‌computed ‌from the ‌displayed ‌form ​itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**d** → ‌**D** ​— ​Same, ​capitalized
- **a** ‌→ ​**a** ​— Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ​**n** ‌— Same
- ​**g** ‌→ ​**g** — ‌Same
- ‌**u** ​→ ​**u** — ​Same
- ​**n** ‌→ **n** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in Hangul ​+ ​Hanja as ​**단군 ​(檀君)** ​— Korean ‌alphabet ​+ Chinese ​characters, ‌attested Modern ​Korean ‌(name attested ​in ‌the Samguk ​Yusa, ​13th c.), ​in ​Korea. The ​script ‌is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

‌The ​scholarly transliteration ‌is ​*Dangun* (Revised ‌Romanization), ​giving the ‌normalized ​reading /dan.ɡun/.

​The ‌rendering proceeds ‌step ‌by step:

- ​Hangul ​단군 ‌with Hanja ​檀君 ​— the ‌founder's ​name as ​recorded ‌in the ​Samguk ‌Yusa

Korean ​names ​may be ​written ​in Hangul, ‌the ‌indigenous ​Korean alphabet, ‌and ​sometimes in ​Hanja, ‌the Sino-Korean ‌character ‌set. For ‌**Dangun**, ​the Hangul ‌form ​is **단군** ​and ​the Hanja ‌form ​is ​**檀君**. Hangul ​‘단군’ ‌and Hanja ​‘檀君’, ​attested in ​the ‌Samguk Yusa ​and ‌Samguk Sagi. ​The ‌ASCII form ​*dangun* ‌is a ‌technological ​compromise; ​the capitalized ​restoration ​**Dangun** is ‌the ‌scholarly citation ​form.

meditation.body:
Dangun ​is named ‌for ‌a ​tree, and ​the ​naming is ​the ​meaning. ‌The sandalwood ​marks ​the place ‌where ​heaven’s order ‌was ​pegged ‌into Korean ​soil; ​the ‘lord’ ​(君, ​*gun*) ​marks the ‌moment ​an ancestor ‌became ​an ‌office. Between ​the ‌two syllables ​sits ‌the ​whole Korean ​claim: ‌that the ‌people ‌descend from ​a ​disciplined ‌animal and ​a ​patient god, ‌and ​that ​their first ‌king ​ruled so ‌long ​his ​reign stops ​being ​a span ‌and ‌becomes ​a climate.

‌The ​restoration of ​the ‌capitalized name ‌is ‌thus ‌more than ​typographic ‌courtesy. An ​ancestor ​who ​lives in ‌altars, ​holidays, and ​divided ​nations ‌cannot be ​flattened ​to lowercase ​without ‌losing ​something real. ‌Dangun ​is the ‌kind ​of name ‌that ‌is ​a charter ​— ​and charters, ​unlike ‌labels, ‌deserve their ​capitals.[^1]

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).
